content: The Guidelines for the Care and Treatment of Persons Diagnosed with Chronic Hepatitis C Virus Infection, published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in July 2018, provide evidence-based recommendations for managing chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection. These guidelines aim to support healthcare providers and policymakers in delivering effective care and treatment, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Below is a professional summary of the key points and recommendations: Background In 2015, an estimated 71 million people globally were living with chronic HCV infection, with 399,000 deaths attributed to complications such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. In 2016, the World Health Assembly endorsed the Global Health Sector Strategy (GHSS) on viral hepatitis, aiming to eliminate viral hepatitis as a public health threat by 2030. This goal includes a 90% reduction in new infections and a 65% reduction in mortality, requiring 90% of infected individuals to be diagnosed and 80% of those diagnosed to receive treatment. Rationale for Updated Guidelines Since the 2016 guidelines, three major developments have influenced treatment strategies: 1. The availability of safe and highly effective direct-acting antiviral (DAA) regimens supports treating all individuals with chronic HCV infection, regardless of disease stage. 2. The approval of new pangenotypic DAA medicines has reduced the need for genotyping to guide treatment decisions. 3. Substantial reductions in the cost of DAAs have enabled rapid treatment rollout in many lowand middle-income countries. Scope and Audience These guidelines focus on the care and treatment of individuals diagnosed with chronic HCV infection. They update the treatment recommendations from the 2016 WHO guidelines and are intended for government officials, healthcare providers, and program managers responsible for planning and implementing hepatitis care and treatment programs. Key Recommendations 1. When to Start Treatment Treatment should be offered to all individuals aged 12 years and older diagnosed with HCV infection, regardless of disease stage, except for pregnant women. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-quality evidence. 2. Treatment Regimens for Adults and Adolescents Pangenotypic regimens, defined as those achieving a sustained virological response (SVR) rate of over 85% across all six major HCV genotypes, are recommended. Examples include: Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 weeks. Sofosbuvir/daclatasvir for 12 weeks (or 24 weeks for individuals with compensated cirrhosis). Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks (or 12 weeks for individuals with compensated cirrhosis). 3. Treatment for Adolescents (12–17 years) Recommended regimens include: Sofosbuvir/ledipasvir for 12 weeks (genotypes 1, 4, 5, and 6). Sofosbuvir/ribavirin for 12 weeks (genotype 2) or 24 weeks (genotype 3). 4. Treatment for Children Under 12 Years Treatment should be deferred until the child reaches 12 years of age, except in exceptional cases of severe liver disease. Interferon-based regimens should no longer be used. 5. Special Populations HIV/HCV Coinfection: Individuals with HIV/HCV coinfection are at higher risk for fibrosis progression. Drug-drug interactions with antiretroviral medications must be considered. HBV/HCV Coinfection: There is a risk of HBV reactivation during HCV treatment. HBV treatment eligibility should be assessed, and treatment initiated if necessary. Cirrhosis: Individuals with cirrhosis, even after achieving SVR, should undergo regular screening for hepatocellular carcinoma. Chronic Kidney Disease: Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir is effective for all six major HCV genotypes in individuals with chronic kidney disease. Data on sofosbuvir-based regimens in severe renal impairment are insufficient. TB/HCV Coinfection: Active tuberculosis treatment should be prioritized before initiating HCV treatment due to the risk of hepatotoxicity. 6. Retreatment After DAA Failure The only approved pangenotypic regimen for retreatment is sofosbuvir/velpatasvir/voxilaprevir. Investigations into treatment failure should include adherence assessment and evaluation of potential drug-drug interactions. Simplified Service Delivery Models An eight-point approach is recommended to support the implementation of clinical recommendations: 1. Comprehensive national planning for HCV elimination. 2. Standardized care algorithms. 3. Integration of hepatitis testing, care, and treatment with other services. 4. Strengthening linkage from testing to care and treatment. 5. Decentralized services supported by task-sharing. 6. Community engagement to address stigma and discrimination. 7. Efficient procurement and supply management of medicines and diagnostics. 8. Data systems to monitor care quality and the care cascade. Public Health Considerations for Specific Populations Certain populations, such as people who inject drugs, individuals in prisons, men who have sex with men, sex workers, and indigenous populations, require tailored public health approaches due to high prevalence, stigma, and barriers to accessing services. Testing Recommendations 1. Focused Testing: Targeted testing for high-risk populations and individuals with clinical signs of liver disease. 2. General Population Testing: In settings with ≥2% or ≥5% HCV antibody prevalence, all adults should have access to HCV testing. 3. Birth Cohort Testing: Testing specific birth cohorts at higher risk of infection and morbidity. Monitoring Treatment Response Sustained virological response (SVR) at 12 weeks post-treatment is used to determine treatment success. These guidelines emphasize the importance of universal access to testing and treatment, the use of simplified and effective pangenotypic regimens, and the integration of HCV care into broader health systems to achieve the goal of eliminating hepatitis C as a public health threat by 2030.
